It's 11 November, St Martin's Day. The children of the neighbourhood are walking through Prenzlauer Berg with lanterns. Jakob is leading his class. Mara and Ludwig walk alongside, with Fritz.
Look at the lanterns, Mara. If only Ingrid could see this! She loved St Martin's Day.
Did you make lanterns too, back then?
Every year, with Thomas and Sabine. Ingrid made the most beautiful ones. If I had tried on my own, they would have burnt down in five minutes.
You know, Ludwig, sometimes I think: what would have happened if I hadn't got the letter from Berlin?
Then you would have stayed in Sibiu. And I'd still be sitting alone in front of the television. And Fritz would have got fat, because nobody but me would have taken him for a walk.
Fritz has got fat anyway. Because of the frankfurters you give him on the sly.
That's a lie. And if it weren't a lie, I would never admit it.
And you? Do you regret anything? Is there something you would have done differently?
Yes. If I had known how little time I had with Ingrid, I would have worked less. I would have gone to the seaside with her more often. I would have played the guitar for her more often.

You needn't be. But I'm telling you so that you don't make the same mistake. The teacher with the cello, who's walking up there at the front with the children and turns round to look for you every two minutes… If I were you, I wouldn't wait too long.
Ludwig! You really do see everything.
Forty years on the tram, child. If I hadn't seen everything, we would all have ended up in a bend.
The stress falls on the participle: “hätte geMACHT”, “wäre geGANgen”.
The old Konjunktiv II forms (käme, ginge, wüsste) are heard mostly in writing. In speech: “würde kommen”.

Unreal = imaginary, contrary to reality. In English: “would…” (present) and “would have…” (past). In German: Konjunktiv II.
You learnt the forms in chapter 23. Now you use them in sentences with “wenn”:

For most verbs: “würde + infinitive”. For sein, haben, the modals and a few frequent verbs: their own form (wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste, wüsste, käme, ginge).
For the past: hätte / wäre (Konjunktiv II) + participle. The choice between hätte and wäre is the same as for the Perfekt:
I would have played the guitar for her more often.
Combination: condition in the past, consequence in the present: “Wenn ich den Brief nicht bekommen hätte, würde ich heute in Sibiu wohnen.”
You can leave out “wenn” and put the verb first (elegant style, especially in writing):

The lantern procession started at five in the afternoon in front of the primary school on Kastanienallee. It was already dark, as always in November, and cold, and the children had red cheeks under their hats. Each class had spent weeks making lanterns: stars, moons, fish, hedgehogs and a very big yellow tram, which Kuba had built, with a little candle in the driver's cab.

Jakob walked at the front with his class, with a guitar round his neck, because the cello was too big for a procession. He played the old St Martin's songs, and the children sang: “I walk with my lantern, and my lantern walks with me.” Behind the children walked the parents, behind the parents walked the neighbours, and right at the end walked Mara and Ludwig with Fritz, who wore a small red light on his collar so that nobody would lose sight of him in the dark.

Ludwig told Mara the legend of St Martin, the way his mother had told it to him. Martin was a Roman soldier. One cold winter evening he was riding through a city gate and saw a poor man sitting in the snow, almost naked, almost frozen. Martin had neither money nor food on him. He only had his cloak. So he took his sword and cut the cloak into two halves. He gave one half to the beggar.

My mother always said: if Martin had kept the whole cloak, he would have been warm, but he would have been alone. This way they were both half warm, but neither of them was alone. When I was a child I didn't understand that. Today I do.

The procession went through the streets of Prenzlauer Berg, past the bakery, where Lena and Andrei stood in the doorway and gave each child a little man made of yeast dough, with raisin eyes and a clay pipe. Past the Mauerpark, where the lanterns moved through the dark like a long snake of light. As far as a little square where a big St Martin's bonfire was burning.

At the fire, Jakob sat down next to Mara. The children were playing, the parents were drinking mulled wine and children's punch, Fritz was begging for dough men. Jakob was holding a mug of tea in both hands and looking into the fire.

You know, if someone had told me five years ago that one day I'd be carrying lanterns with twenty children in Berlin, I would have laughed. I would never have left my village if my grandmother had still been alive.
And do you regret it? Leaving?
No. If I had stayed, I wouldn't have met Kuba. And I wouldn't have read his essay. And I wouldn't have met Jonas at the choir. And then I wouldn't have…
He stopped. Mara waited. The fire crackled. Somewhere behind them children were laughing. Then Jakob said, very quietly, without looking at her: “Then I wouldn't have met you.”

Mara looked at him. She thought of Ludwig's words: if I were you, I wouldn't wait too long. She thought of Ingrid, who had waited three days at a stop, and of Lena, who had asked Andrei at four in the morning what he was still waiting for. She thought that in three years in Berlin she had had so much courage for other people. Just never yet for herself.
Jakob. Would you have time on Saturday? For a coffee? No choir, no children, no dogs?

Jakob turned towards her. In the firelight, Mara saw that he was smiling, so broadly that he almost looked like Kuba when he got praised. “No dogs is going to be difficult,” he said. “Fritz is sitting on my foot right now.” Mara looked down. It was true. Fritz was sitting on Jakob's foot and looking up at him, as if he had already adopted him.

At that moment Kuba came running up, with his tram-shaped lantern, whose candle had just gone out. “Mr Lorenz! Mr Lorenz! My tram isn't burning any more!” Then he saw Mara sitting next to his teacher, saw Fritz on Jakob's foot, saw the two faces in the firelight and stopped. Kuba was ten years old and he wasn't stupid. He looked from Mara to Jakob and back. Then he said, very seriously: “If you get married, I want to be the witness. After all, I introduced you. With my essay.” Jakob choked on his tea. Mara laughed so loudly that half the class turned round. Ludwig, who was standing a few metres away, pretended not to have heard anything, but his shoulders were shaking with laughter.

On the way home, Ludwig walked next to Mara, slowly, with his stick, and said nothing. Only in front of the door did he stop. “So, Saturday,” he said. Mara went red. “How do you know?” Ludwig shrugged. “Fritz told me.” Then he went in and hummed an old song on the stairs. A song he hadn't hummed for fifty years. The song he had danced to with Ingrid in 1974.

On Saturday they met in a small café on Kollwitzplatz. Mara arrived ten minutes early, which had never happened to her before, and Jakob came five minutes early, with a small bunch of asters in his hand that he had bought at the market. They drank coffee for two hours and talked about everything: about Thuringia and Transylvania, about children who didn't want to do their homework and patients who didn't want to take their pills, about his grandmother's cello and her father's bees. When the waitress asked for the third time whether they would like anything else, they realised that the street lamps had already come on outside.

Jakob walked her home, through the dark streets, and this time they didn't need any excuse. In front of the door he asked her whether next Thursday, after choir rehearsal, she would go out to dinner with him. Mara said yes, without thinking twice. Then she stood in the courtyard for a long time under the chestnut tree, whose last leaves were rustling in the wind, and thought about what Ludwig had said: if I had known how little time I had… Up on the fourth floor Mrs Hoffmann was playing, and on the first floor the yellow lamp was burning. Mara thought that she didn't want to regret anything. Not in fifty years, not in five years, not tomorrow. And that this time she hadn't waited too long.
On the kitchen table the autumn flowers stood in an empty honey jar. It was the last of the three jars her father had packed in her luggage three years ago.

Reading text: St Martin's Day in Germany
Read about this German tradition. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
On 11 November, many children in Germany celebrate St Martin's Day. They make lanterns and walk through the streets in a procession in the evening.
The day commemorates Martin of Tours, a Roman soldier who lived more than 1,600 years ago.
If Martin hadn't shared his cloak, the beggar might have frozen to death.
Today children often get a little dough man or a St Martin's goose after the procession. In some regions they go from house to house and sing for sweets.
The most important message of the festival is simple: sharing warms you.
